Research task, read-only. Do not edit any file in D:\Atharva\firstrun or D:\AccuKnox\help. Write your result ONLY to D:\Atharva\NOTES\PROJECTS\NeatHack - 10 October\33 Real World Targets.md (this is a private planning folder).

Context: FirstRun is an agent that takes a quickstart docs URL, turns it into shell steps, runs each step in a fresh python:3.11-slim (or node:22-slim) Docker container on Linux with network on, finds the first step that breaks, patches it, and drafts a docs PR. For the hackathon demo we want 4 to 5 REAL open-source docs sites whose docs source is in a public GitHub repo, so a found break can become a real PR.

Pick candidates by these rules:
1. Docs source is public on GitHub (name the repo and the exact file path of the quickstart page source).
2. The quickstart has 10 or fewer shell steps and runs on Linux in a container with no paid account and no API key (or a free key is optional and skippable).
3. The tool is known to developers.
4. Prefer pages likely to have drift (old version pins, renamed packages, removed flags, Python version issues) - read the page and judge.

Slot 1 is fixed: the AccuKnox help docs. Local clone at D:\AccuKnox\help (upstream AccuKnox/help). Find the best quickstart-like page there that runs in a Linux container without an AccuKnox account (for example a CLI install like knoxctl / accuknox-cli, a Helm-free install check, or a getting-started with a public tool). Give its public docs URL (help.accuknox.com/...) and the source file path. If no AccuKnox page can run without an account or a Kubernetes cluster, say so honestly and name the closest one plus what step would block.

Then pick 3 to 4 more from projects such as: FastAPI, Typer, httpx, Pydantic, uv, Ruff, MkDocs, Poetry, LangChain, LlamaIndex, Chroma, Qdrant client, DuckDB, Polars, Streamlit, Flask, Django tutorial part 1, Hugging Face datasets, Ollama (no), Prefect, Dagster, dbt-core (dbt is relevant: Atharva works at Altimate AI), Marimo, Litestar. Exclude neatlogs, Entire, Chroma getting-started (already used).

Use the Firecrawl CLI (`firecrawl scrape <url> --format markdown`; if out of credits run `python D:\Atharva\NOTES\SCRIPTS\keys\keys.py activate`) or WebFetch to read pages, and `gh` to confirm the repo path (gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/contents/PATH).

Output file format: a ranked table (rank, project, quickstart URL, docs repo + file path, step count, needs key?, why drift is likely), then 2 backups. Then one line per pick naming the exact URL to feed FirstRun. Keep it under 60 lines. Report back in 6 lines: the picks with URLs.

# Writing rules, the only set

Applies to every word you output: chat, emails, docs, copy, code comments, commits.
Generated from `DIGITAL TWIN/rules/` (one file per prose rule) and `SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py` (the regex tables). Do not hand-edit this block.
Edit the source and rerun `python SCRIPTS/slop/rules_prompt.py --write`.

Verify with `python SCRIPTS/slop/score.py "<file>"`. CRIT must reach 0.

## A. Punctuation

1. Em dash (—): use a comma, a period, or rewrite the sentence
2. En dash (–): use a comma, a period, or rewrite the sentence
3. Double hyphen (--) as a dash: same as above
4. Semicolon (;): split it into two sentences

## B. Sentence shapes that are always wrong

5. Never write "not only X but also Y".
6. Never write "it's not just X, it's Y".
7. Never write "it isn't X, it's Y".
8. Never write "not X, but Y" or "not X, but rather Y".
9. Never chain "no X, no Y". Name the one thing that is missing.
10. Never chain "did not X, did not Y". One negative statement is enough.
11. Never write "Do not call it X. Call it Y." Just call it Y.
12. Never write "the X is real, and ...". Give the evidence instead of the word "real".
13. Never end a sentence with ", highlighting the ..." or ", underscoring the ...". Make the point in its own sentence, or cut it.
14. Never write "that is the whole point" or "X is the entire game". State the point.
15. Never write "the whole point is ..." or "the entire game is ...".
16. Never write "that is the part ...". Name the part.
17. Never write "my favourite part of ...". Say what it does.
18. Never write "the only X I trust". Say why the others fail.
19. Never write "the only thing that matters". Rank the things.
20. Never write "that is why X mattered". Show that it mattered when it happened.
21. Never write "that is the real problem, and ...". Same tell with a noun wedged in.
22. Do not land a sentence on a bare negated verb ("The data did not."). Finish the clause.
23. Do not open a sentence with "Honestly," or "Look,". Announced sincerity is not sincerity.
24. Do not close a line on "X is dead". Say what replaced it and when.
25. Never write "X is dead, long live X".

Every rule from here on applies ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English. Apply them coarse to fine. Each rule names its file in `DIGITAL TWIN/rules/`, which holds the reason and an example.

## C. Shape the piece

26. Put the answer, the action or the claim in the first line, inside 40 words. The condition and the caveat come after the answer. (`start-with-the-point`)
27. Open each section on its own claim. Cut a first sentence that would fit under any other heading. (`every-section-opens-on-its-claim`)
28. Write every H2 in AP Title Case, with no colon, as the claim the section proves. Lowercase only a, an, the, and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet, as, at, by, in, of, off, on, per, to, up, via and vs, and capitalize each part of a hyphenated word. "10,000 AI Agents Cracked a 90-Year-Old Math Problem in 88 Hours" passes. "The problem" fails. (`headings-state-the-claim`)
29. Size the label to the beat. A long section takes a heading, a medium beat takes a bold lead-in, and a short beat takes no label. (`label-each-beat`)
30. Put a blank line between beats, and keep each beat to a few lines. A paragraph runs six sentences at most, and four is better. (`write-with-whitespace`)
31. Push detail down under a summary line, and keep the top level short. The top level alone must read as the summary. (`nest-dont-flatten`)
32. Make a list when a sentence names three or more parallel items. Keep prose when the sentences build an argument, or when there are only two items. Give every bullet the same grammar. (`lists-or-prose`)
33. Split a list of more than five items into a few labeled groups. (`group-a-long-list`)
34. Number a list only for steps in sequence, a ranking, or items the reader will cite by number. Use bullets for everything else. (`number-only-when-ordered`)
35. End an open list of examples with an item that covers the rest. Leave a closed set, such as the members of an enum, closed. (`leave-room-for-the-unnamed-case`)
36. Bold at most one term per beat. Inside SUBSTACK/, never bold or italicize a word mid-sentence. A bold label that opens a line is allowed there. (`bold-one-term`)
37. Cut a paragraph that adds no new fact, and merge two paragraphs that make the same point. Cut the closing recap. (`length-is-not-depth`)

## D. Break the sentences

38. Put one idea in each sentence. Never let a sentence contradict the one before it. (`one-idea-per-sentence`)
39. Keep sentences to 20 words or fewer. A procedural step is one action in one sentence. (`twenty-words-max`)
40. Give every sentence a finite verb. "That is the problem" passes. "The problem." fails. Build rhythm through sentence structure, never through fragments. (`every-sentence-has-a-verb`)
41. Mix short and long sentences inside the 20-word limit. (`vary-sentence-length`)
42. Write "because", "so" or "but" between two linked sentences. (`state-the-logical-relation`)
43. Name the thing in the sentence that uses it. No dangling "it", "all four" or "the best one". (`name-every-referent`)
44. Never make the page, the table or the paragraph the subject. No "here is the honest limit", no "a table follows". (`no-narration`)

## E. Cut the words

45. Write one or two reading levels down. Use the short plain word, keep the precise technical term, define it the first time, and reuse that exact term. (`say-it-plain`)
46. Cut a sentence that helps the reader decide, build, remember, check or understand nothing. (`every-word-is-a-debt`)
47. Cut a sentence that could move unchanged into another piece or product, or make it specific to this one. (`cut-what-could-go-anywhere`)
48. Cut a quotable line that carries no fact you can point at, and keep the number. (`no-clever-one-liner`)
49. Cut an adjective a reader cannot check, such as "powerful", "critical" or "key". Replace it with the fact behind it. (`cut-the-empty-adjective`)
50. Use one word for one thing, every time. Never swap in a synonym for variety, such as "check", then "verify", then "confirm". (`one-word-one-meaning`)
51. Use active voice, American English, and a named human actor. Write instructions as commands: "Run the scorer", never "the scorer should be run". (`active-voice-named-actor`)
52. Write the action as a command. "Make sure the valve is open" becomes "Open the valve". (`state-the-action-not-the-wish`)
53. Turn a noun back into its verb. "Make a decision" becomes "decide", and "conduct an analysis" becomes "analyze". Watch for -tion, -ment, -sion, -ance and -ness. (`kill-the-hidden-verb`)
54. Make claims with numbers: "4 years", not "a long time". Cut the hedge, but keep honest doubt such as "I do not know why this worked". (`be-specific`)
55. Write positive statements. No double negatives, no "not unlike", no "fails to avoid". (`write-positively`)
56. Use present, past or future. Avoid the perfect and progressive forms. (`simple-tenses`)
57. Keep "the" and "a". Write "the build fails", never "build fails". (`keep-the-articles`)
58. Cap noun strings at three words. Break "content team output metric" into a phrase with a verb. (`short-noun-strings`)
59. Say the literal action. No idioms, no slang, no metaphor that carries the argument. (`no-idioms`)
60. Drop a comma that changes no meaning. Keep one that stops a wrong reading. (`cut-the-optional-comma`)
61. Write in first or second person to "you". No emojis, no preamble, no generic introduction. (`you-and-no-preamble`)

Writing jobs also load the craft profile: `python SCRIPTS/slop/rules_prompt.py --profile craft`.

## F. Banned words and phrases (60 words, 169 phrases)

score.py holds the full table and the writing-gate hook blocks the write on any entry in it, naming the exact one it caught. So write the sentence you mean and let the gate catch the rest.

These words are worth avoiding up front, because a model reaches for them without being asked and a blocked write costs a round trip: delve, leverage, robust, seamless, ensure, comprehensive, elevate, empower, streamline, utilize, groundbreaking, testament.

The banned phrases fall into three shapes, and section B already states most of them as rules. The first shape announces a point instead of making it. The second promises the reader something interesting before delivering anything. The third pads a sentence with words that carry no fact. Say the thing itself and all three disappear.

Run `python SCRIPTS/slop/score.py "<file>"` to see the full table applied to real text.

## G. Banned headings (20)

A heading names the claim inside its section, never the outline slot it fills. These exact headings are CRIT:

  background, challenges and future directions, closing thoughts,
  conclusion, final thoughts, final word, in closing, key takeaways,
  legacy and impact, overview, summary, the bigger takeaway,
  the bottom line, the call to action, the key takeaway, the takeaway,
  who this is for, why it matters, why this matters, wrapping up

## H. Advisory, flagged but not blocking

score.py also flags soft words, hedges and flow problems: a sentence over 20 words, monotone rhythm, passive voice, three sentences opening on the same word, a verbless fragment, a paragraph over six sentences. MED and LOW never block a commit, so treat them as a second opinion rather than a rule. Run the scorer to see which ones a given draft trips.
